utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By switching on my microphone, I merely wanted to continue or, rather, to complete my submission around MFI 576, and that was why I stood up. By your leave of course, unless you had something you wanted to raise beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it this will be short, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I promised that I would take five minutes only, and now my learned friend, Mr. Moore, asked that I delay this discussion until tomorrow because Mr. Weiner, who is not present here today in the courtroom, was the one who is informed of the issue. I wish to tell you that I spoke to Mr. Weiner personally because I wanted to reach an agreement concerning this matter of MFI to be admitted into evidence. However, they tell me that they challenge the authenticity of the interview of Mr. Hadzic. Therefore, the OTP challenged the statement as such and are opposed to its admission into evidence. For this reason, I will then agree to what my learned friend has suggested and that is that we discuss this matter tomorrow because then we will have the occasion to hear what their reasons are for which they are opposed to the admission of this document into evidence. That is why I move that we wait until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well then. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Domazet, your client is not able to be present again today. I see there is a consent to -- filed from your client for the trial to continue today in his absence. That is the position, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, indeed, that is the case. Mr. Vasic spoke to Mr. Mrksic over the phone and Mr. Mrksic told him that due to some swelling that he has, the doctors advised him to be bed-bound until next Monday. I know that, indeed, he signed a consent for the trial to continue in his absence. Based on what Mr. Vasic told me, my client does not agree to the following witness being examined outside his presence, but perhaps we can deal with this a bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We have a consent for today to proceed. We will do so on that basis. You have now your next witness ready, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Witness Gluscevic is ready. Pursuant to the relevant order, I will be examining the witness within the time frame you defined, which was half a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Domazet has some questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gluscevic. I will be examining you on behalf of the Defence for Mr. Mrksic. As I already indicated in our proofing yesterday and today, please let us make a pause between questions and answers. Please observe the transcript in front of you and wait for the text to finish so that the interpreters can catch up with us. First of all, Mr. Gluscevic, introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber and the other participants in the proceedings, your full name and other personal details?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borisa Gluscevic. I was born in Kamena Gora, Prijepolje municipality, Serbia. I completed the military high school in 1962 in Sarajevo. It was there that I served for one year. I graduated from the military academy of the ground forces in Belgrade in 1967. Thereupon, I was posted to the Bileca garrison, which is what is today Republika Srpska. This was an infantry school of the then Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia or, rather, of its army. I spent nine years there, serving the duty of the platoon commander, number 5, for two years, and I was the general tactics teacher for two years. In 1976, I went to Belgrade to undergo training at the command staff academy of the ground forces. I spent another two years there. Having completed my schooling, I became teacher on the subject of general tactics at the military academy of the ground forces in Belgrade. I spent teaching there for -- I spent teaching there 11 years. On the 12th of September --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or Interpreter's correction: On the 20th of September, 1989.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order, of course, I took up the duty assigned to me at the Guards Brigade. It was then that I met Mrksic for the first time. My duty was that of an assistant to the commander of the Guards Brigade for logistics. That was the official title. And that was my official title until my retirement. I carried out this duty at the Guards Brigade also during the Vukovar operation, which meant that I had been carrying out this duty two years before the operation and continued carrying it out afterwards. As I was carrying out this duty, pursuant to an order, I was appointed chief of logistics of the corps of special units of the army of Yugoslavia, and I carried out this duty for seven years until the units themselves, the special units, were disbanded which was in 1999. And the last two years before my retirement, I held the duty at the logistics sector of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia at the operations institute as chief of department for operations and logistics duties. On the 30th of June, 2001, I was retired, and continued living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic, for this information. In short, you have described your entire career up until your retirement. I will go back to the relevant part of your career, relevant to us. You told us what your duty had been in 1991. Can you just tell us, please, what rank you held in the army at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: As of the 22nd of December, 1990, I was colonel and continued holding that rank for 12 years before Vukovar, after Vukovar, and it was with this rank that I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the deployment of your unit to the Vukovar area, namely what your duty had been, what your tasks had been, and where you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: As the assistant for logistics, my duties were quite sensitive, since I had to prepare our deployment to Vukovar. It was -- it fully depended on the quality of the organisation of the logistics; that is to say, the active units were fully dependent on us. It was on the 30th of September, I believe, but don't hold me to that, I'm not really certain about the dates, and besides, all the records existed, although on the 4th of April, 1999, it was particularly the military files that concerned me that were destroyed in the bombings. That was why I cannot in fact confirm. It was in the NATO bombing. Therefore, units set out and then spent the night at Sid and the following day I arrived in the territory of the Vukovar area, namely the village of Berak, at the brigade base, where I set up a logistics command post with all the requisite elements that such a base entails. Throughout the time, ever since my arrival in Berak, up until the 24th of November, I was stationed at this particular location and never left the area except to go to Negoslavci from Berak. On average, I had at least once daily phone and personal contacts with Mrksic when he was at his command post. I went to report to him as did all the other commanding officers. Normally it took place in the late afternoon and we reported on the previous 24 hours. If I happened to come across him in the morning hours, then I would report to him then. And he would then relieve me of the obligation to come to him again in the afternoon or evening hours to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic. If I've understood you correctly, you did not leave Berak to go anywhere else but Negoslavci up until the 24th of November, and that included Vukovar, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you would go at least once daily to Negoslavci normally in the afternoon hours, sometimes in the morning. These afternoon meetings, were they official briefings of commanding officers? Can you describe them for us?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Domazet, reporting is a customary practice in the army, both in peacetime and in wartime. It is normally carried out at a fixed hour every day, and all commanders are duty-bound to attend these meetings, all the commanders of subordinate units, that's to say assistant commanders for logistics, moral guidance and so on and so forth, unless one had good reasons not to attend them. The meetings had fixed agendas. First -- the first ones to report were combat unit commanders. They also had many questions to ask of logistic commanding officers because their activities involved the spending of a great deal of ammunition, materiel, equipment and so on and so forth, and it would be toward the end of the meeting that they would express their requests that they had of logistics commanders. Colonel Mrksic would, on the basis of the discussion held, issue specific duties and tasks to every single commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. As I see, your presence there was indispensable in view of the activities your units were charged with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said the meetings took place in the afternoons, just before nightfall. Do you know, was there a fixed hour for these meetings, or would the time of the meetings vary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friend now I think three times has said afternoons. The witness actually said late afternoon and my learned friend has not operated on that basis, and now we are moving on to before nightfall. The witness should be allowed to give his own estimate of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. I hadn't noticed and still don't appreciate any major movement. But carry on, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Gluscevic, tell us something about that. To the best of your recollection, when were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I cannot say exactly after such a long time but I think that they took place at 1700 hours, or perhaps 1730 hours. Now, why? Only due to security measures so that we would get it done and over with as soon as possible and that we would go back to our units and give them orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Can that be seen from some documents?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: But of course. Probably from the operative logbook which was kept regularly at the operations room at the command post of the corps, and I could also proffer my own documentation, if it could be present here today. We would see that from the work notebook and there would be no dilemma as to when these meetings were held, what was said at these meetings and who said what at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about you personally? Did you record in that diary of yours not only the time and date of the meeting but also who said what and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Everything that had to do with me and my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gluscevic, I will go back to -- or, rather, I'll move on to almost the very end of your stay in Vukovar. If necessary, we can go back to some things that happened even before that, but what I would like to do here and now is to ask you about things that I consider important. Do you remember on which day Vukovar fell, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I couldn't remember that, that would mean that I was very, well, well, how should I put this? Well, let me better not say anything. So of course I remember. The 18th of November. I myself found out sometime between, say, 14 and 1500 hours, if you're asking me very precisely. And I was pleased. I was pleased, because it was a great burden off my shoulders. That's how I felt. There will be no more fighting and no more equipment would be needed, so it was a great sense of relief that I felt then, and also I was happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I hope I understood you properly, that at first you said that you did not go to Vukovar at all. So even on that day and after that you didn't go to Vukovar? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you say yourself that you remember that date very well, I'm going to ask you whether you remember a meeting, if it was held on that day, with your superior officers in Negoslavci. Was a meeting of that kind held and, if so, do you recall such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, a meeting was held, and it was held sort of in an abridged fashion, if I can put it that way. It was quite clear to all that there was a sense of relief. Mrksic chaired the meeting, and since all the results, so to speak, could not have been seen yet, then in principle, well, I'm speaking in general terms now, he gave some instructions as to what would follow in the coming period but without any details, because he could not have -- well, it was just that moment, and I think that we were done very quickly and then we all went to our respective units to make sure that discipline was still there, if you were ever in that situation, then you know what a commander says to his subordinates in that situation, so that nothing undesirable happens in terms of consequences and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, what you have been telling us just now, I mean when you say these instructions, these orders, and about these undesirable consequences, what was all of that about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this. We have had three 65 ter or two 65 ter summaries. We had a proofing note today at 12.30, and there is no reference in any of those documents about any meeting on the 18th. There is no reference to it on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wasn't talking about documents and I wasn't asking about documents. I asked about what the witness was telling us about in his previous response. He was talking about what Colonel Mrksic had said then. As for the proofing, it is correct that today, well, not at 12.30 but at 12.00 exactly, as soon as I finished speaking to the witness, I submitted what I had to submit, and it says in the proofing notes that these orders would be referred to as well, these orders issued by Colonel Mrksic. I don't want to repeat this in front of the witness now but my learned friend received this and, indeed, this does exist in the proofing notes. There is a sentence about this. So these are not documents but verbal orders that the witness started talking about during his previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I have not seen this proofing note. On the basis of what was previously distributed, I would suggest the evidence should commence on the 19th of November, and deal with the 19th and 20th in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, that is exactly where we were, the 19th. I'm going to move on to the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Gluscevic, whether on the 19th a meeting was held and do you remember that meeting if it was held?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. On the 19th and on the 20th and on the 18th, we had these meetings or briefings, or this reporting, and quite a few tasks were spelled out concretely at these meetings. That is to say that for me, as assistant commander for logistics, most of my assignments had to do with technical matters and what was stressed was that I should get ready and the logistics battalion in the brigade base and that the moment had come for us to soon hand over these duties to other units, new units, and that we would go back on furlough or to get some rest or recovery. That is what I could say to you in the briefest possible terms. I told you, if I had the documents I could read it all out to you for each and every piece of combat equipment and so on and so forth. There were quite a few details there but I mean, well, I don't think we have to go into these details because I don't think I could really say everything, but for me as assistant commander this involved quite a bit because this was the result of 60 days of war. Quite a bit of technical equipment was destroyed, also it was all over the front line, all of this had to be brought back in, and to say the truth, we were happy that that moment finally came. When I say "we," I mean logistics. Probably others felt that way too. That we would get out of battle. That we wash up a bit, tidy up. Things like that. 60 days without our families, it was really quite difficult and quite strenuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic. You talked about the 19th of November, the day after the fall of Vukovar and the meeting held on that day. Now I'm interested in the next day, that is to say two days after the fall of Vukovar, the 20th. Do you recall that meeting with the officers?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that meeting. Oh, and I've had a countless number of details from previous meetings and other meetings that I could recall but I am just going to refer to one particular detail, that is perhaps of interest to you and others here. I can only say that this meeting was chaired by Colonel Mrksic. It was the customary type of meeting, that is to say customary briefing in the same order as usual, but also there was some information. There was some new information provided there by our subordinates in terms of what had been done on the previous day, with war booty and I don't know, the ill people, and also a certain equipment that had to do with the quartermasters' units. When the meeting was coming to a close, as I was there in my capacity as assistant commander and I was sitting very close to him, I had reason to put a few other questions to him as well, of course in relation to logistics and resolving related problems, nothing special, nothing else, really. And at that moment, well, I mean the meeting was over and people started going their own ways, and as he was giving me some instructions, in relation to some technical equipment, specifically tanks, how to resolve that, where to take them, how to get them out and so on, at that moment, on the door of the operations room, there was Captain Mile Bozic, and Mrksic immediately reacted to that and he said, "Mile, if necessary, take -- if necessary, even a company of APCs and help them over there around Ovcara." At that moment I considered that to be irrelevant, and I can say with full responsibility that after that, we continued for about 20 minutes more to discuss our logistic problems. Well, perhaps not 20 minutes but it is for sure that for about 15 minutes I was discussing matters with him, that is to say, the many logistics problems that we were facing and that we had to resolve in some way. There were a lot of damaged tanks there, and you probably have some of this information. I mean, I would have had very accurate information, precise information otherwise. I mean, I don't want to say anything that would be wrong or untruthful in terms of the numbers, how many tanks were destroyed, how many were damaged, what we would do with the trucks and vehicles and this and that and so on and so forth. And then when I understood what he was saying and when he understood what I was saying and when he gave me some instructions regarding the handover of certain elements to the 80th Kragujevac Brigade, I mean, that I should not be tight, so to speak, with the equipment that the Guards Brigade had, that I should give them jackets and warmer clothing and so on and so forth. It was getting cold and that I should give them what they needed. So our conversation evolved along those lines. And then in that operations room now who else was there? Was it only the duty officer or someone else? I cannot confirm. I mean maybe some other officers were there too. But anyway, we went our separate ways then. I went to talk to my own officers there, I had two of them. If it is necessary for the Court, this is Captain First-Class Danko Jovanovic, and my first assistant for operations well, my, he's not mine, it's Major Petar Todorovic. But I mean in terms of the chain there, he was there in my unit. So during the Vukovar operation, during my free time, so to speak, during the day most of my coordination took place with them. Do this, do that, have a look at this, have a look at that, and so on and so forth. Then perhaps I spent some 15 minutes with them and spelled out certain things in very specific detail, how things would evolve that day, the following day, rather, and then went back to Vukovar. I cannot say with any degree of certainty what time this was, but I'm sure that for security reasons, it was between 1900 and 2000 hours. That is to say, everything that I've been saying so far was concluded by then. I went back to my subordinates who were waiting for me there. Of course, they were eager to hear what the commander was asking us to do and whether we would go to Belgrade soon. That's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have to go back to some things a bit because you gave a bit of a lengthy answer. And you described practically your entire stay there up to the very end of that meeting. So I will have to take you back so that you would deal with some of these matters yet again. And could you please respond slowly and could you keep your answers as brief as possible, please? You mentioned the 80th Motorised Brigade. Do you remember who the commander of that brigade was?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Vojinovic"]. I met him even before Vukovar fell. I mean, we were discussing logistics matters. I was with his people, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, did he attend the meetings at the command that you attended as well, every day?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I think so. No, it's not that I think so. He did. That evening, as for that briefing, I think, well, it's not that I think, as far as I can remember, it's very hard to say today after all this time, I cannot speak with 100 per cent certainty, but Mrksic introduced him and said that he would be responsible for the Vukovar zone and that we would move on to new assignments that we did not know about yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that, that Mrksic introduced him as the person who would be responsible for the Vukovar zone, what meeting are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I think that he introduced him at that key point on the 20th when we knew him quite well. I mean, he got quite a bit of equipment from my base over those few days. If you ever served on the reserve forces, you know the reserve forces come in with trousers and boots that are too small and so on and so forth. So I don't know exactly when he came but I think it was, say, around the 10th. I cannot say for sure. So he sent his own quartermasters and technical support people to link up with my own people and we were together in Berak, and I think that that's how it went. Or, rather, it's not that I think that; that's the way it went. I claim and assert that that's the way it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you directly -- well, you did talk about it a bit, but my direct question is: On the meeting of the 20th, was Lieutenant-Colonel Vojinovic there too, in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I've already responded. It's hard to say today, but with 90 per cent certainty, not more than that, I can claim that he indeed was there. Because in that period, when we were going our separate ways, I wasn't the only one who walked up to Mrksic. Many people did. And others like him perhaps too. There were things that were unclear and people put extra questions. So I think he was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were talking about the subject of that meeting, that is to say what was discussed at that meeting. However, if I understood you correctly, you were actually talking about what had to do with your own unit and that's probably what you remember better. Do you remember at all anything else except for what you told us just now, Captain Bozic, do you remember any briefings by other officers, whether any other officers reported to Colonel Mrksic, or do you remember such things or do you not remember at all?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not really say anything that would be of interest in actual fact. I mean, if we had my work notebook here, then you could have a look at it, too, and perhaps you would even laugh at all the things that people reported about. But now, today, saying something, well, I really don't know. I'm not in a position to -- well, every commander ultimately asked through Colonel Mrksic that the logistics people do something for them. And that was a bit of a stress for me at every one of these meetings. Because there was not a single briefing without the logistics battalion being referred to, and that is what really stayed in my mind as far as these meetings are concerned. I took down what other commanding officers were saying as well. I mean, these are my former students, if I can put it that way. I knew them well. I spent years with them in school and sometimes I would ask them a few things. I would sort of say why they were asking for this or that, or why they were reporting in such a way. So that's the kind of thing I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You relayed to us what Mrksic said when he saw the captain in the doorway. Can you cast your mind back and tell us whether this was at the time when all the officers were still in the conference room or had they all gone by then?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, at this point in time, the meeting came to a close but the people hadn't left yet. Normally -- I could actually compare it to the situation where you have a lecture that you're holding and then you close it and then all the students go out and some walk up to the teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us what these words uttered by Mrksic were or who they referred to?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who was it who first raised these matters. I can only assume that it was to do with the problems connected to prisoners, civilian population, the matters that were mostly in the foreground at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Captain First-Class Bozic, the person you mentioned, who was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Captain Mile Bozic, who passed away unfortunately, he was killed in a traffic accident in Montenegro near Pljevalji, I don't recall when this was, was there in his capacity as commander of the 1st or 2nd Military Police Company of the 1st Military Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he have APCs within his ranks?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Military police companies had APCs, and we used to refer to them as guards' APCs. These were combat vehicles for infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us that you walked up to Colonel Mrksic at that time to raise the matters you mentioned. Was there someone else with you whilst you talked to him or had the conference room gradually emptied and you ended up alone with him? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Practically, the meeting had not yet ended for me. I don't know how familiar you are with military matters, but what we normally do is in order not to tire everyone else with matters that are not relevant for them at such military briefings, the commander tells those present to raise these matters at the end of the meeting. The meeting room was full of people. People lit cigarettes and then slowly walked out. I don't think anybody was following what we were discussing because these were matters that had to do with me. And of course these soldiers, they know how these things work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you might have mentioned this but I will ask you again about this conversation between the two of you. Do you know how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: At least 20 minutes, perhaps even more, because we had a great deal of matters to deal with. And of course this was something that would not be noted down in my private notes or in my work notes that I had. Perhaps we even argued about certain matters because my position was such and such and his was different. So it may have gone like this: Colonel, shall we solve this in this way? And then he would say no, I believe it should be dealt with differently. These were some crucial matters concerning logistics support that had to be solved within the framework of an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know or not if you would be going back to Belgrade? And I mean at the time of this conversation you had with him.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No. Our discussion had to do with military equipment and with what was to come next. He would tell me, Borisa, or, rather, no, he would most often refer to me as Gluscevic. And he would say, "Gluscevic, we'll see about that, we'll see how these matters will be solved."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us that having ended this conversation with him, you left the room and then met with some colleagues of yours. Did he leave the premises as well?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: The meeting room and his own office is within that same building. I suppose that maybe some of his operatives may have been left behind and perhaps they discussed matters or left. I went to a house that was about 100 metres away where I had these associates of mine, my assistants, and I spoke to them and stayed there for some 15 minutes, I don't know, and then I left. This surely was before 8.00 so it may have been 7.30 because by 8.00 I had to be at Berak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You've mentioned Berak just now. I have to put this question to you again because I'm reading something in the transcript but I just want to double-check whether you said this, in fact. Where did you -- how did you leave Negoslavci and where?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I used an old truck and I went to Berak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- it states at some point in the transcript that you went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No. I apologise. It's a mistake. It must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You did not definitely go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of some testimony we had here, on that same evening, did Colonel Mrksic come to Berak as well, before you arrived there or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry not to see Mr. Mrksic here today. It was only once in these two months that Colonel Mrksic came to Berak, and that was in early November. Never again did he go there. I would see him every day, and he probably didn't go there because he didn't have any problems with logistic support. I will say this but you can ask him. He had great confidence in the entire structure dealing with the logistics support for these units. Nobody lacked equipment, fuel. We were very efficient in repairing hardware. Since the brigade base or, to put it simply, the logistics battalion had a lot of equipment in stock, he would come over to see about that and to procure the equipment. Also, there was a -- there were extra personnel and manpower. So whenever you needed a cook or you needed a butcher or someone because they would not be there at the front line any longer, he would come over see me and other chiefs to discuss these matters, to bring the strength of manpower up and that would be it. And I'm sure he didn't go there because had there been any need, he would go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm content with your answer, but nevertheless I have to put the following question to you: Had he come over on that night or some other day, would you have had to know about it? Would it have been possible for him to come there without you knowing it?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I would have known it. It was a village with only several roads. Both ends of the village were covered by check-points that I personally observed. It would be impossible for a commander to come to the place where his assistant is without letting the latter know about it. And why would he go and check like this? There would have had to be a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned Mrksic as your commander. You said that you had been a member of that brigade for two years before the Vukovar operation and you stayed there afterwards. As an officer whose superior was Mrksic for quite a long period of time, what would you be able to tell us about him in his capacity as commander?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, it was for history's -- the truth's sake that I came here. I can tell you that I don't know whether Mrksic appreciated me or not. You have to ask him that. But I have respect for him because of the following reasons. He was not -- he wasn't rash. He did not bully his subordinates. He did not put people down. And I can at least speak for myself. We, I think, started trusting each other quite soon because as soon as I came there, he did not really accept me right away. It was probably in time, as he saw the performance I had in my work, he grew to respect me and, you see, I'm the sort of person who doesn't mince his words. And I can tell you all the people, his associates around him, could not hold a candle to him. This is perhaps a bit rude, might sound disrespectful to others, but I can tell you that Mrksic is a great person. And I'm sure that if you went to talk to every single member of the Vukovar Brigade, all of them would only support and confirm what I've just said. And I mean the Guards Brigade members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me, were you and Colonel Mrksic friends? Were you on visiting terms?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I had never heard of Mrksic before I came to the Guards Brigade in that month of September. I had been a professor at the academy, and I wasn't that pleased to work in the field, to have to spend time in the boots, and I particularly wasn't that pleased with the department that I was to deal with, the logistics support, having been a teacher myself. In this period of time, I was the chief of logistics support in the corps. My, you see, position was such that I would even envy those persons who he referred to by their first names or nicknames, whereas he always referred to me as Colonel Gluscevic; Colonel Gluscevic would do this, would do that. He never used the familiar expression. He always addressed me with V and not with the personal T in the B/C/S. And he kept this distance, and that's why I appreciate him and have respect for him as a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, but my question was were you on visiting terms? Did your families visit each other? Were you friends?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never on visiting terms with my superiors, with my bosses. I had many such superiors in these 40 years of experience and I never became that intimate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just briefly go back to the commander of the 80th Brigade. Can you tell us what his family name was? I believe it was entered incorrectly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there when he was christened but probably his name is Vojnovic, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now it's correct. Because the earlier name in the transcript was Vojinovic and that of course is a bit different. You said that it was on this meeting that he was introduced as the future commander of the town. Did his units in fact take over the command of Vukovar and did you have any commitments in this regard?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me simplify my question a bit.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Don't call these meetings. These were briefings. Meetings were the gatherings when Mrksic was there. With him I didn't have meetings of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You talked about that time when it was said that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic would become the future commander. Did you and your units have any obligations in assisting him in this handover?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure when exactly that was but you can find that in the documentation, in the orders and documents that certainly state this clearly, but you can see there whatever dealings I had with him pursuant to Mrksic's orders at the time they were deployed there. First, they had to be supplied with -- with wood. Through my quartermaster service he was supplied with a quantity of wood from Karadjordjevo. Next, they had to be -- and also with trucks, so they also had to be provided blankets, clothing and so on and so forth. Although of course he came from a different place so he had to be given technical support from us. I don't see this as quite that important to tell you exactly what my dealings with him were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I wanted to hear about the period following his arrival there. I would like you to look at two documents now, Exhibits before this Tribunal, and I have questions for you concerning those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 425. Could we have that one on the screens? Mr. Registrar, please? And could we first look at the bottom part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Gluscevic, could you please read the last two paragraphs in this order that is right in front of you where it says "during the course of the day"?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: "During the course of the day, all measures were taken so that the 80th Motorised Brigade would take over the organisational and command functions in the area of responsibility of the Operative Group JUG, South. The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade" -- I'm sorry, I misspoke. "The command of the 80th Motorised Brigade received all instructions and documents for organising command and control in the area of responsibility of the Operations Group JUG, south."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What does this mean, what you read out just now? Does it mean that this 80th Brigade had already taken over all of these responsibilities or not?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: It means what I already said a few times here. The 80th Brigade took over everything. They had everything in their own hands, and we were there practically just to prepare for what followed on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just in a single sentence, what was it on the 24th? What was it that followed?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Those who are familiar with the army and equipment and technical aspects, a brigade with 700-something vehicles cannot set out immediately. So in the period from the 22nd and the 23rd, we completed certain activities and then we set up marching columns on the 24th, probably in accordance with orders issued by the superior command, and then we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we remove this exhibit and then my examination is coming to a close. But first I would like to have 415, Exhibit 415, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have the document in front of you. Can you please have a look and could you tell me whether you know about that document? Do you recognise this document or not?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You know what? It's hard to say now what happened 15 years ago but I can say only, but with full responsibility before this Court, as far as I can see, this is a document from the command of the 1st Military District, from the forward command post. Therefore, all documents that come from the -- that came from the forward command post to the Brigade command were distributed, if necessary, as they were, to the subordinate units, that is to say to the assistant commander for logistics as well, and our documents were based on them too. That is to say, our orders and other documents. And I believe that had all of this been kept in the archives as I've said a few times already, had all of this not been destroyed, we could have found this document and its trace from the command to the brigade base, to the logistics post, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Gluscevic, that we could follow this trace, it seems to me that on the basis of that answer that you've already provided that this should be either this order or an order based on this order. Do I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understand me right. But this -- I mean, the Operations Group South, JUG, should fully act in concert with the tactical and so on and so forth, all of that would have to do with the combat units, first and foremost, and probably the commanders of the 1st and 2nd of the Guards units and so on, it probably had to come in a different form. I mean, Mrksic's order had to arrive. And this copy could have reached me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've let it go for sometime. We use -- the phrases being used that indicated it's pure speculation, phrases like "probably," "probably," "could," in my submission, either this witness has seen this document or he has not seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, could you get from the witness what he actually knows about the document, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, that was my question, actually, whether he's aware of this document or not. Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't debate about it. Just move on and deal with it with the witness if you would. We are not interested in him trying to work out what it must be but about anything that he knows. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Gluscevic, you heard this. You see this document now, and perhaps you see a bit more of it right now. Do you know anything more about this document, very briefly, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I can say -- I mean, I'm sorry, I apologise to the Court. I was talking about documents in general. I cannot say anything about this document. I was talking about documents in general, how their trace could be followed, because I saw up here that it was the command of the 1st Military District, and I thought that the question was based on how these documents came in. I was trying to clarify how documents went to subordinate units, if I can put it that way. As for this particular document, I cannot say anything. I don't recall it. It had nothing to do me. There is no reference to me here or to anyone of my people. As I said, it only pertained to the combat units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic. Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic. I have no further questions for you. I would like to thank you for your answers, and I would particularly like to thank you for the fact that you came nevertheless in spite of your personal problems and family problems, that you came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my examination and I tried to fit into the time that we specified. I think that I started at 2.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask -- well, either to consult my client for a minute or should we take the break now and then perhaps I could put my questions? Perhaps I just have one or two. He's already signaling me now that he has no questions but I wanted to consult him in relation to something. I probably would just take a minute or two of your time, if I were to ask anything at all but we could have the break first. No, sorry, sorry, sorry, I didn't realise. I thought that this was the time for the break. I see that the time for the break is only in 15 minutes. Sorry about that. Can I just have a moment to consult with my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you first speak to lawyers about giving evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I first saw Domazet yesterday, about twice I talked on the phone over the past 15 days. I talked to Vasic three or four times altogether, from when the proceedings started. I mean, if you're interested, perhaps I could say it's been, say, two years. I wasn't noting anything down, but Vasic was the first one who got in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be right to say, then, that when you were speaking to the lawyers, and we will deal with Mr. Vasic and Mr. Domazet, you told them what you could say, what evidence you could give, to assist Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't put it that way, Judge. When talking to Vasic, that is to say the first time I talked to him, a long time ago, in Belgrade, in Nusiceva Street, I don't know the exact house number, I said that I could give a statement in terms of how certain things were that he asked me about at the time, and quite truthfully so, because I remembered them. That's how it all ended. After a while, he again consulted me with regard to certain matters. I also directed him to talk to some other officers who knew about this better than I did. And at any rate this cooperation between him and me went on until, say, about a month ago, along the following lines, that I would make a statement. Because there are different reasons why I couldn't come here. And if I can put it that way, in a way, I was promised that, but the time came that even in my old age I would have to get a passport and come here nevertheless. It's not a very pleasant thing taking this long journey but I've come here to say the truth and nothing but the truth and no one can convince me of anything else. What I have said is the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you just try and keep your answers a little shorter? But I come back to the initial question: Did you explain to Mr. Vasic or indeed Mr. Domazet in terms or in substance what you could say, what evidence you could give, in relation to the case of Mr. Mrksic? Is the answer yes or no, or could you give it in those two words, please?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So did you discuss, then, what had happened at the meeting on the 20th, with Mr. Vasic or Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, what had happened. Nothing had happened. I mean -- I mean, we weren't making any such comments. Specifically what the lawyers were interested in, like today, is what they asked me about. And as for some concrete things, well, you know, he would say, was this this way, was that that way, and then I would say it was that way or it wasn't that way. That's the only kind of discussion we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. But in reality, the evidence that you are giving here principally deals with the meeting of the 20th, when Mrksic is there and there is reference to I think his name is Captain Bozic. That's what the guts of your evidence is about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I mean Bozic is mentioned in the context of -- I mean, Judge, Your Honour, when I mentioned this Bozic now, when I spoke previously, I said that at the moment when I was writing in my notebook, he showed up in front of Mrksic and I wasn't interested in that at all at the time. But I came to say what Mrksic's reaction was. He said to him immediately, Bozic, if necessary, take even a company of APCs and go and resolve that. Perhaps he also pointed to this Vojnovic. I mean, at that time I wasn't interested in it at all. I only had my own work to do, and I think that that has been said loud and clear. I don't see any reason why we are going back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the reason is actually perfectly clear. It's because I want to know when you first told Mr. Vasic about Bozic. Simple. And could we have a short answer, please?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'll tell you that. The first time when Vasic -- not only in relation to Bozic. I mean, when we met in Nusiceva street, say two years ago or whenever, that is what I said then. Now, how Vasic understood this and what he understood, I'm not going into that. But as far back as then, I mentioned Bozic, because that's what was being talked about, that event, and then I said Mrksic was with me, I said. He was telling me about some tanks, what I should do and so on. All of a sudden Bozic appeared and he said to him, quite harshly, I told him about some details, what Bozic looked like, a big man, and one -- I'm 1.000 per cent sure that that's the way it was then. That's what I said to Vasic then. I mean, I did not say that only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you see, we have a problem here in this trial because we have been going now for a lifetime, approximately a year, and this is the first time that anybody has mentioned about Bozic. We've had witnesses come and give evidence about that meeting and that name has never appeared. You are the first person who has ever mentioned him. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Now I understand, after what you have stated, but I mean I don't really mind, it doesn't affect me, because I know this Bozic was there, and I know that Mrksic gave him such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It goes a little further than that. Normally, when witnesses give evidence, what is suggested to them is what actually happened. So, for example, let us say, Mr. Vojnovic gave evidence and I'm quite sure you know he did, nothing was ever said to him, "By the way, Vojnovic, we would suggest that it was suggested that Bozic should get a number of armoured personnel carriers and go and sort out Ovcara." Nothing was ever suggested about this at all. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Judge, I'm just surprised that you don't believe me. But I state to you with full responsibility that I'm not interested in what Vojnovic said here or anybody else. I came here to say what was heard at that moment in front of Mrksic or, rather, what I learned then. I mean, I don't know why you insist on it that much. If this Bozic were here, he could confirm that but unfortunately he's not here. He's not among the living any longer. But my work notebook could support that and many, many other things even more. I mean, I'm not saying that it would say in the work notebook Bozic said such and such a thing, but you could see that this conversation took place between me and Mrksic and, well, how should I put this? It just so happened he came there. I mean, I'm not assuming how it was that he came but it is 1.000 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So, of all the people in all the world who could have helped Mr. Mrksic, Mr. Bozic, he unfortunately is dead, and of all the documents that could help you, they have unfortunately been destroyed. Is that -- is that a correct summary of it?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the one who is to judge who can help Mrksic. That is probably in somebody else's hands. I'm here to speak the truth and nothing but the truth. I have said the truth and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told this Court that you've told the truth about five times. Can we just move on to what you were supposed to have said? You see, we got summaries, we got one on the 10th of August, we then got what's called an amended summary on the 6th of September. And I'm going to go through these documents which really are statements of what we were expecting you to say. Now, in the first document, there is absolutely no reference to your attendance at the meeting on the 20th. All there is is, so I read it out to you, "He will testify to the manner of regular informing in Negoslavci, especially to his observations in the periods of the 19th, 20th of November while he was at OG South command post in Negoslavci." Not a single reference at all to you being present, about references to Ovcara, references to Vojnovic, references, more importantly, to Bozic. Not a single word. Now, can you explain how that has happened, even though you perhaps did not create the document. Nothing is there.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Judge, sir, it is inconceivable to have any kind of reporting without the presence of the assistant commander for logistics. Now, who was it that gave you this information that I would not be there, that I would not be present? I mean, that is the mainstay, and all the commanders and all the subordinates move within that circle because without logistics you cannot have fuel, you cannot have vehicles, you cannot have any such thing. Who was it that could have been there if it weren't for me over there in Negoslavci? If you've learned anything about the military, you've got to know that this is a basic thing. One cannot wage war if logistics doesn't function properly. That is a response to what you said. As for the rest, who did what and in that context, who wrote what, I mean, I cannot respond to that, because I, as far as I know, did not provide any such thing to you. Now, who provided whatever is something I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What you're really saying is that when there are meetings at the command headquarters, there are certain officers who will always be there. For example, commander of logistics. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Not only commander of logistics but all who are along this direct communication line with the commander. They can only be absent if he gives his approval. But then a deputy would have to stand in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that presumably would apply to the chief of the security organ. He would be another person. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I can say what the general rule is, and probably it should apply to him too, but now I mean, well, don't keep putting all please questions to me. Let my statement remain as it is. All of those who are along this direct communication line with the commander, and the book shows who is along this direct communication line and who has to attend these meetings and briefings. You have the books and they clearly show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And they clearly show that the chief of the security organ would normally be there at the meeting of the command headquarters. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: He would be present unless the commander assigned him a different task to be elsewhere, or if another superior of his issued him with an order requiring him to be elsewhere. That's the general rule in the military. He would be present unless there was a special reason for him to be absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we put it this way, that in actual fact if he wasn't present, he would delegate, the chief of the security organ would delegate someone to stand in for him so that the security organ would be represented? That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Listen, that's a very sensitive issue. I can only tell you the following: When I am required to be elsewhere, then Colonel Stojkovic, who is my first subordinate, will stand in for me. As for the chief, I don't know what the rule book says with regard to his duty. I can speak for myself. Every commanding officer of a certain unit has his entitlements, duties and obligations specifically defined. This includes the person he has to report to. If the chief is not present, then this is something that the commander must definitely be aware of as he would be the one to give his consent for his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you trying to be truthful here? Are you trying to help the Court?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That being the case, would you agree the security organ is a crucial component in relation to command structure and operations with the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No. All of us are important. How can he be more important than me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we work on the basis that you're all terribly important?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that joint command, all of us are terribly important or equally important, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the statement that we have, you say that you have no idea why it is that the meeting of the 20th is not specified in the first summary of the 10th of August. So we have heard your evidence on that. What you were actually going to give evidence about was your meeting with General Jerko Crmaric. Do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Listen, General Jerko Tomanovic is being mentioned here. There is no such person. There is General Jerko Crmaric. Tomanovic is a quite a different person -- or, rather, I don't know about General Tomanovic I know about Dr. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is this little piece of paper with two paragraphs deals with your ability to give general information and then a meeting with General Jerko Crmaric. That was all we were going to hear evidence about. Now, I want you just to listen for a moment, if you would be kind enough. We then got a second summary from the Defence dated the 6th of September. Now, I accept that on the document dated the 6th of September, there is reference to Mile Bozic. I accept that. But I would suggest to you that the account that you give in this document is different in many fundamental ways from the evidence that you have given. So I'm going to read through various parts and get you to explain how it is that there are differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court has got a copy of this supplementary note. Might I respectfully inquire if the Court has? Because it's a 65 ter summary supplement and it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dated the 6th of September, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page 1 only. It's numbered 8. It appears to be continuing on but we haven't that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, it was a composite bundle and this only relates to this witness. The other pages referred I think to other witnesses. I hope I'm right on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a line and a half on the next page which fortunately I now have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is the first reference to the fact that you didn't want to go into to give evidence. I'm not going to ask you any questions about this. Second paragraph relates to the fact that you're the assistant ware commander in Berak. I'm not going to ask you about that. Third paragraph relates again to the topic about General Jerko Crmaric. I'm not going to ask you about that. Then there is another paragraph, I'm not going to ask you about that. But I'm going to ask you now to the substance of what is said. First thing I want to ask you is this: Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just curious, because you seem to be looking at the screens.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't understand a word. Except for Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll start, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know about the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are letting you run on a moment or two, Mr. Moore, because I thought you were at a point that might be reaching a climax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, regrettably not a climax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, in that event I think we need to have a break now because you only have two or three minutes left on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn and resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with what you are or were going to say. I'll read it out. "He will testify," the he is you, "to the circumstances which arose from the testimony of Milorad Vojnovic and with respect to the regular reporting at Negoslavci on the 20th of November at the command place of the OG South." So far so good. "On that occasion, after Milorad Vojnovic reported the problems that occurred at the hangar at Ovcara in the course of that afternoon and that he managed to solve and overcome the problems that he induced full control at the hangar." Now, here is a reference to "after Milorad Vojnovic reported the problems occurred at the hangar at Ovcara." Well, we haven't heard any evidence here in your evidence about Vojnovic reporting problems, have we?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not just a case of asking. It's a question also of giving evidence and telling. You can't just pass the buck to somebody else. You're here to give evidence. You were asked actually two or three times by Mr. Domazet to tell us basically what happened in that meeting. And not a tickly-boo was said about Vojnovic reporting problems. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, when I was preparing myself for the testimony and thinking about what I would say, I had the intention of simply saying the truth. I don't know what Vojnovic said. Had he said something which had to do with me I would be able to tell you that Vojnovic asked me, and perhaps in fact he did, whether the elements that he had in the -- the elements that I had in Berak of the Guards Brigade, whether they would stay behind or not. I'm certain that these matters were discussed, as is stated here, but I cannot tell you what it was that Vojnovic talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, no. In this summary, it is quite specific. It says: "After Vojnovic reported the problems" and goes on "that occurred at Ovcara, he managed to solve and overcome the problems." So it is -- the word is "reporting." Therefore it deals specifically with the problem, and the fact that Vojnovic had overcome the problem and that the problem was at Ovcara. Now, there are three specific references in that account and yet you didn't mention any of them when you were giving your evidence. So how do you account for those three omissions?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I made any omissions. Whatever you asked me about, I gave you my answer. I suppose that if you had been in my shoes at the time -- please put yourself in my shoes and try and picture what was happening there. Not just on that particular briefing but the briefings in the days preceding that day. I told you how things worked and what we got, and I don't think that there was reason for me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have asked you specifically about the 20th and the three references. Will you please direct your answer to that question? What is your answer? How is it there are three specific references which you have not mentioned in your evidence, even though you were given many chances by the Defence who are calling you? Why did you not mention problems? Why did you not mention Vojnovic reporting problems? Why did you not mention Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Why would I be mentioning them? First of all, I was never at Ovcara. Second, Vojnovic had no other points of contact with me except for that -- for being at the same briefing there. What else? What is your further question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll move on to my next question. Colonel Mrksic stated that problems like those must never occur again and that if needed, Colonel Vojnovic should ask the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, to allow use of the armoured transporters company headed by Mile Bozic. Now, I will go through this particular statement as well. Mrksic stated that problems like those must never occur again. You have said nothing about that at all in specific terms when giving your evidence to this Court, have you?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't because there was no mention of the commander, and I don't know when it was that he said that, and I mean Mrksic, when he mentioned these matters and where. He did not talk to me about those matters. He talked about the ways in which I could pull out the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, no, no. This summary is what your evidence is supposed to be. This is the 6th of September. There is reference to: "Colonel Mrksic stated." "Stated" in English means "spoke." "Colonel Mrksic stated that problems like those must never occur again. And that if needed, Vojnovic should ask the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, to allow use of the armoured transporters company headed by Bozic." Are you saying then that you never heard Mrksic say this? Is that what your evidence is now?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Listen, I can't say that I heard him stating that. I don't see why you're asking me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking it because this is a document which we are told reflects your evidence. It's a document that's created by the lawyers of Mr. Mrksic, usually on the instructions of the people that they speak to. Are you saying that this is a false document, that this does not accurately reflect what you told them?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. I stated what I stated and I stand by my statement. And I meant concerning Mrksic, Bozic and myself. Now, what Mrksic stated where, I don't know, and don't try to put this to me in such a way that I should answer and say that it's untruthful. I can't say whether it's the truth or not. I can only talk about my interactions with Mrksic in the presence of late Bozic. And of course I can answer any other specific questions you may have for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I'd suggest that's not right either. Did you see this document when you came to speak to the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Which document? Can you show it to me? I'd like to see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I've got an English. And I'm terribly sorry my B/C/S is not quite what it should be.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't speak English. I know -- I can only speak Serbian. I have seen no other documents but the military documents shown to me. I don't know if the document you are referring to is a military document. I didn't see any other documents but different orders, reports and operation log books, things that I'm familiar with as a military person. I don't know what it is that you're showing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think or I would suggest, not -- my views aren't important. I would suggest that you know perfectly well what I'm asking, that this is an account given by you, translated into English, as apparently reflecting the evidence you are to give. This is not a military document. This is a document which reflects your anticipated evidence. Now, were you ever shown such a document or not? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't give any statement anywhere. I only talked to lawyer Vasic, as I've already said, and yesterday with Mr. Domazet. It was the -- it was yesterday afternoon that I saw him for the first time and I told you that I spoke to him, but I didn't give any statements or have before me any documents of the sort. I said that Vasic showed me some orders, operations logs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the reference that Colonel Vojnovic should ask the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, to allow use of the armoured transporters, where has that come from? Where has the name Miodrag Panic come from? Because it's a very specific function, when you are Chief of Staff. So where has the Chief of Staff reference come from?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Listen, the only person next to the commander to engage all units, including brigade units, is the Chief of Staff. That was the authority he was vested with by the legislature. You're asking me about Miodrag Panic and what he was told or what he said. I don't know about that. I only know that he had the authority to issue orders to me in addition to Mrksic, and he was the only one because Chief of Staff under the establishment is the deputy of the commander, although I know that he did not issue any orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But that's not what I'm asking. I'm asking a very simple question. May I finish? That in this reference, which is supposed to be your anticipated evidence, you're supposed to have heard Mrksic saying, "Speak to Panic." Because he will allow you to use the - may I finish? - to use the armoured transporters headed by Bozic. I'm asking you where has the reference to Panic come from?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Listen, you're asking me a lot of things. I told you what Mrksic told Bozic. Now, whether at this point or a bit later Mrksic mentioned the Chief of Staff, that he was supposed to sort this out with Bozic, I don't know. My head was full of other matters that I had to deal with and it's been 15 years. I can give you no answer whatsoever to that that would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I haven't quite finished on this one. There is no reference at all to any conversation with Bozic. Only "Speak to Miodrag Panic who will refer to you Bozic." There is no reference to Bozic being present, no reference to a conversation with Bozic, whereas your evidence says he pops his head around the corner and suddenly gets lumbered with an order. So how do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying -- well, I can explain that very well, because it remained impressed in my memory, etched in my memory, in fact. Besides, I thought that this was the particular moment where there were officers who were able to hear this. Now, whether Panic was involved, I don't know. However, I can tell you that what I stated with regard to Bozic is 1.000 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We normally find 100 per cent is adequate in this Court. Can we just move on to your proofing note? We've got a proofing note which came to us today, somewhere between 12.00 and 12.30, and this apparently was as a consequence of your conversation yesterday. We'll just go through that, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does the Court have a copy of the proofing note, may I respectfully inquire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to put that before the Court so that they can understand the cross-examination. But at this time I don't ask for it to be made an exhibit, merely for understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please pass up the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can put it on Sanction which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have a copy of that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you gave your evidence about what happened, and I want to refer to the second paragraph. Here we are, we've got Colonel Mrksic presenting Vojnovic, the future commander of Vukovar. Now --

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This means nothing to me. This isn't in the language I understand, my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I can read it out to you, if you wish, and it could be translated. Will that help? I'll have it read out to you in B/C/S. "The witness will give evidence in respect of regular daily meetings at command post of OG South in Negoslavci, especially at the time of the fall of Vukovar and with special emphasis on a meeting held on the 20th of November, 1991, when Colonel Mrksic presented Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, as the future commander of Vukovar." You agree with that? No problems? Next paragraph: "The witness will testify that at the time the meeting was about to conclude, and all officers, including Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, were still present in a room, Captain First-Class Mile Bozic entered the room and Colonel Mrksic reacted loudly and said, 'Bozic has armoured transporters. If needed, use them and make them go away.'" All right? Now, that's what your statement says.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not really the case. I stated here the way it was. Mrksic and I seated -- were seated next to each other. At that point, Bozic appeared at the door and probably - I say probably because I can't speculate - Mrksic told Bozic the following: "Bozic, if need be, you can take a company" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, what I'm asking is really very simple. Your evidence today is the fourth version of what we have heard, or what's been presented to us, and even this one there is no reference to Ovcara, just a reference to "Bozic has armoured transporters, if needed use them and make them go away." Now, why is there no reference to Ovcara? Why is there no reference to problems?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You should ask someone else that.
