At the time, I, and I believe my colleagues, too, did not see -- I'm sure that this were problems, as some of them raised them, but I believe that at the time of the briefing, if we want to really analyse and examine the briefing, there were problems, but they weren't so much in the foreground. To you, of course, they are now very important, but at the time these problems were not made that topical. We had many such instances where soldiers were put under great pressure and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean that at the time these problems were not that topical, you had many such instances? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant to say the following: At that point in time, Ovcara was not -- and not just to me but to most of the people there, was not -- well, we were preoccupied with our own problems. I had 700 to 800 soldiers and 700 to 800 vehicles in the brigade, and that's where my problems lay. If Vojnovic arrived there and raised some problems, then this must have been problems that were crucial to him and not to me. I only thought of my problems and not of other people's.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were other problems occurring at that time where soldiers were under pressure from the local TO with regard to misbehaviour?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: In Berak, my people, no. Let everybody speak for himself. In Berak everything was fine. That's where I was. I wasn't in Berak at that time but I was at the command post in Negoslavci, and I had no pressure whatsoever in Berak. Everything was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm asking you were you aware that there were other problems occurring.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: What other problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Problems where soldiers were under pressure from local volunteers or TO who were misbehaving?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You know what? From this vantage point, I cannot, well, probably I wrote something down in terms of highly organic matter, but I cannot say anything to you with certainty now I am aware of such and such a thing. I could not put it in such decided terms. I mean, perhaps, had they come up with something stronger, I may have remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about this statement: "I only thought of my problems and not other people's. If Vojnovic arrived there and raised some problems then it must have been problems that were crucial to him and not to me." So I'm asking to you whether in actual fact there were problems being raised at meetings or mention was being made of problems that were occurring with TOs and volunteers but obviously not in Berak?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether problems of the TO were being mentioned in relation to that, I mean, that has to do with logistics, well, yes, but if you're asking about something else, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then what did you think was meant, "Bozic, take some armoured personnel carriers over to Ovcara and sort it out?" What did you think that meant?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, today I can say what was thought. Probably that some unsettled situation should be taken care of. But at that time, I didn't think anything, to be quite honest, nothing. I was just waiting. And actually, I was upset because he barged in that way and interrupted my conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when the Court considers your evidence, and it's the sentence that you say is the true sentence, "Mile, if necessary" -- "take, if necessary, even a company of armoured personnel carriers and help them over there around Ovcara," what is this Court to make of that statement? What is it supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that that moment I mean, well, if I mean, if it can be put that way, what happened at that meeting and after that meeting. Now, who is going to understand this, in which way, the Chamber, anybody else? You know what, I was a teacher for many, years and not only from that period, I remember a great many things, remember them very well, although I'm 63 years old, and in an initial story, I told that to Vasic, not yesterday, not today but two years ago. That's what I said then. And then what happened after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to go on with this a little further. There is reference -- perhaps I read it to help you. "The witness particularly remembered that all of them who were present heard that, including Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. The officers started leaving, except the witness," that's you, by the way, "who remained in order to discuss the task of his unit with Colonel Mrksic and that discussion lasted or another 15 or 20 minutes. After that they both went out and separated." Now, we have heard Vojnovic give evidence, nothing was ever said to Vojnovic about "Bozic, go and get your armoured transporters," nothing has been said about Miodrag Panic, and we also have had another witness called Vukosavljevic, security organ from the 80th. He gave evidence and he gave evidence that he spoke to Mrksic after that meeting broke up, immediately after the meeting had broken up. Now, did you see somebody else coming in with Vojnovic speaking to Vojnovic at that time? Because it would be in the time when you were allegedly there.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: That first part of your question or text, when you say did somebody else hear or, rather, that somebody else did hear, I assert that what happened at that moment, when the meeting was over, I, Mrksic and what he said to Bozic, that could have been heard by half of the room and seen by half of the room, but let's be quite honest about this. Did it occur to anyone at the time to write that down? I mean, I was just there. I don't know whether Vojnovic heard it. You should ask him. Whether some third person heard it, I don't know. But really, it is pointless to ask me. I mean, they could have heard, like you can hear what we are saying now. It was a small room, like next to -- like up to those pillars up there. I mean, really, I have told you what I said, and that's it. And now as for the rest that you've been asking me about, I mean, well, I mean, why Panic is being mentioned, I don't know. I mean, you've been going back to that. You should ask him and who mentions him, well, have him brought here and ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You see, so there is no misunderstanding, what I'm suggesting is that you are a gentleman who has come here to lie, that there are four separate and different accounts given by you and you're having difficulty actually remembering what was said on those previous accounts.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Judge, if that is what you're saying to me, I can tell you, quote a famous quotation, well, never mind. When a person says something to another person, if there are no arguments for that, then it applies to the other person. Do you really have arguments to that effect that I'm lying? I mean, don't discredit me that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is no reference to Miodrag Panic. There is no reference to Ovcara. There is no reference to conversations in your earlier -- in your earlier statements. There is no reference to Bozic. Nothing. And yet you come here and suddenly we have evidence that covers 15 to 20 minutes when you leave and covers Bozic going to Ovcara. I'd suggest those are the reasons I'm accusing you of telling lies.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Me? I said that about Bozic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting you have never mentioned Bozic for some considerable time and when you have, the story has changed three times.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: It did not change at all. Look at the first, second and third one. It's always the same. I said that Bozic went to Ovcara? Is that what you said just now? No way. I never said that at all. No, no. I did not even mention Ovcara or Panic. I mean, please now, don't plant that on me. Well, please. I mean, I know, well, I mean, I can take quite a lot but, I mean, when did I say that? Have a look at what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then, how did the name of Panic get into this particular summary? Because it's your summary.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you asking me that? I never mentioned that, Panic. Not a single time. Now, find that place where I mentioned Panic. Show me that document. Now, I mean don't come up with this stuff written by somebody else. In what I stated here today did I ever mention Panic? I don't like to mention him, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And tell me, did you ever sign a statement or produce any documents prior to coming to court or coming to The Hague this weekend?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I take it that means no? I have nothing on the translation.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not sign any statement before coming to The Hague or in The Hague. I just conducted a conversation with a lawyer, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if a record was kept of that conversation with the lawyer, would you be prepared to let me see that document? If you're telling the truth, you have nothing to fear, have you?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Notes kept by who? You mean me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. Sometimes when people have a conversation with lawyers, lawyers are terribly active and they make notes, and I'm asking whether in actual fact notes were made of the conversation with you. Now, if they were, would you be prepared to let me see those?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: How can I permit you something? I mean, I never kept any notes, in all these conversations, today, yesterday, two years ago. And it's not that it really bothered me in any way. I mean, now I'm a retired person and I did such a lot of writing during my career. I wrote textbooks and I wrote notes, and now, I mean, well, if somebody took some kind of notes, Mr. Vasic, Mr. Domazet, you talk to them. I haven't got any notes, and I have no military memories or mementos, because everything was destroyed in my office, and I'm so sorry about that because there was lots of literature there and other things that have to do with the 40 years I spent working on that job, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say -- I've noticed that you use the word "I only speak Serbian." Forgive me for being simple. I sometimes know it as B/C/S, Bosnian, Serbian, Croatian. Is that the same language?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you it's Serbian. Now what you know I really don't know. Maybe it's the same. I'm speaking the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have heard of Seselj, the politician?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How would you describe his political orientation?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to answer to that at all. Although I completed the political school of the Yugoslav People's Army, I'm not taking an exam today to give answers about Seselj and his political orientation. If that is the topic of this conversation, you should have told me and I should have done a bit of studying and I should have prepared for this. I'm not prepared for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Giving evidence is not like a box of Leonida's chocolates. You just don't pick out the ones that you like and disregard the rest. You understand? Now I want to ask you the following question: Do you agree or disagree with what Seselj's political views are?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. That is not a question for me. I'm a soldier, a professional. Ask me about my profession. Ask me anything you want from my profession. I'll give you answers to that. As for this Seselj. First of all, I've never seen him, ever, except on television, and I don't see why that question cropped up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. I think that this question is not based on the examination-in-chief, and it cannot have anything to do with the witness's statement and his credibility. I really think that it goes beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Moore, it is not obviously on point. Have you had enough or do you want to persist with the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll not persist but I would like to pursue the area. It has two relevances. One in relation to the 13th of November and second to a document that I may show this witness in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will try and be brief on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you accept that Seselj is an extremist and that he has extreme views and had extreme views in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Judge, not a word on that question. Seselj is not my superior officer. He's not a like-minded person. He's probably a Serb like I am but nothing else. Don't ask me about that. I came here on account of my colleagues with whom I participated in this. You can ask me about that. Don't ask me about Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you that you're a gentleman who supports an extreme Serbian view, just like Seselj?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You can never ascribe that to me. I was and remain a Yugoslav and a Serb. Throughout the former big Yugoslavia, if I were to stroll about Ljubljana nowadays for about two hours somebody would walk up to me and say hello to me, greet me. I spent over 17 years in different schools and I know people. The same thing would happen to me in Skopje or Zagreb or Sarajevo. I have many friends belonging to all the different national ethnic groups. I can prove that time and again. Not only here. If you were to take me to Ljubljana or to Skopje now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about Croatia? We have heard the defenders of Vukovar, the Croatian defenders of Vukovar, as being described as terrorists in 1991. Do you agree with that, them being described as terrorists?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Who described him? Who was it that described them? Let me see, who described them as terrorists. I don't know about that. Terrorist this and that. I mean, now you are going into a political topic and you're asking me about some things that are peripheral as regards this. Now, what is the point? What is the objective? Are you trying to provoke me? Are you trying to put words in my mouth? To say things that have nothing to do with my very own personality or is it something else? I don't know. But I see no reason why you are moving in that direction, things that don't really have much to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've almost finished. I will move off this topic. The security organ, what is the function or what was the security -- what was the function of the security organ in November 1991 and at the time that the guards were at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, you're asking me a great deal. If you asked me what the role was of the assistant commander for logistics, namely me, perhaps I could remember -- well, I wouldn't rattle it off like a pupil, like my Radic did a long time ago, but I can say just like you, he's responsible for the security of the brigade and nothing more than that. There is nothing more I can add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it a case that the security organ is what I will call very hands-on, that they are aware of what's going on?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was never a security organ. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you can suggest, I would suggest, because you know perfectly well that the security organ were always involved around and about Operation Group South.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean that? All of us were involved in questions that had to do with Operation Group South. I told you a few moments ago, he's not more important than I am and I'm not more important than he is. We all worked as a team. A command is a good team. I don't see that somebody was involved more than somebody else. What was important for me as assistant commander for logistics certainly wasn't important for him, because he had his own line of work, but we got along very well, and we cooperated in terms of contributing both ways. Now what you're trying to ask me about security organs, I mean, I was never with them. I cannot say. I know that they did their job well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you have dealings with Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Always. It was excellent. I'm sorry that we cannot greet each other properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that Sljivancanin was an officer who was involved in the general -- when I say "control," I don't mean it in a military sense. That he was involved around the activities of OG South, as you would expect from the security organ?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: You know what, Judge? Sljivancanin was a major. He was chief of security, as you have put it in your question. This is the second time that I'm telling you that he was involved as much as I was; involved meaning that he did his job, I did my job. Now, where we had points in common, then we would sit down and talk. We all know on what subjects. He could give information to me if he had some better information, not only in Operation Group South but also during the many years of our work. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest that, as I've already done, you have come to deliberately mislead this Court, that you have given various accounts on various occasions, and that in actual fact what you have told, I'm afraid, has been a tissue of lies to help your colleagues. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said what I have to say to that. When a man says something to another man and he doesn't have arguments, then the same goes for him. If you have any arguments that this is untrue, show me these arguments. Since I have been disarmed, so to speak, if I had my work notebook from Vukovar, the one that I kept for 60 days as a teacher and as a logistics man, probably you would have less ability to try to provoke me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions but I would wish to make an application for the summaries prepared to be made exhibits, going to the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have they not be the sufficiently the subject of cross-examination to identify the material passages, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I put it this way? Clearly there has been cross-examination on it and on what I will call the important areas, I hope. Nevertheless, in my submission, it often assists if the full documents can be present so that the Court, when considering the matter of credibility, can look at it with more precision and without perhaps the same difficulty as one would have when looking from a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll leave that matter for the moment, Mr. Moore. You've made your motion. Mr. Domazet, first, at a critical point in cross-examination, you stood. I signalled to you to sit down. I want to be sure that that's on the record so that you have it recorded. And the reason I signalled to you is that the point of cross-examination appeared then to be critical and it would have disturbed it to intervene and interpolate something. Is there some matter that needs to be raised at this point before you re-examine arising from that or could whatever you have in mind, if it's still important, is it better left until after your re-examination has finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was really patient when Mr. Moore was putting his questions, the same question several times. That and also some leading questions, and he's entitled to that. I rose then, well, doesn't really matter, but it seemed to me that at that moment the question put to the witness was that the witness had said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, if you're going to deal with this matter in re-examination, you should deal with it first before saying something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. That will not be the case at all. I have just a few additional questions during my re-examination. That will not be a topic at all. I'm not going to go back to that at all. I just wanted to explain why it was that I then -- well, since the witness gave answers. After that, it was no longer relevant. I don't know whether at this point in time I should state my views in relation to this motion just made by the Prosecutor, namely to admit the summaries into evidence. If so, I can respond very briefly. I'm opposed to that. It pertains to the previous summaries as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I suggest you re-examine and then we'll deal with these other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. Gluscevic, that are based on your answers given to Mr. Moore. One that intrigued me was, in your answer a few moments ago, I think it was on page 54, you said I think, or I may be mistaken, you said "my Radic." Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: I taught him for two years. I was his teacher for two years and that's why it just came out. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No need to be sorry. I just asked because that was not the subject of any one of our conversations. You also said at one moment when you were giving your answers I think to what was said about Panic, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic. I wrote this down, you said: "I don't like to talk about Panic." Could you please say what it was that you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, it is an ugly thing that we are forced to a say ugly things about our own people, but within the context of today's discussion I mentioned two officers of mine, one being Danko Janovovic, who is an administrator with the operations and technical -- I apologise to the interpreters. With the operations technical organ, and Petar Todorovic who was an administrator for the rear in the Guards Brigade. I don't want to mention Panic, not because I have anything against him, or he against me, but he is a Chief of Staff and you should call him as a witness. I don't want to be the one mentioning Panic and then to have to see him here tomorrow. But if you have something regarding Panic and his relationship to Gluscevic or Mrksic and that this is being -- this is important for the proceedings, by all means call those people to come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I just wanted to have this clarified because I thought you had some special opinion about Panic because you had an opinion about Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I said he doesn't even -- that he cannot even hold a candle to him, but I don't want to speak ugly about my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since the better part of the cross-examination was concerning what you told to Defence attorneys, I have only a few questions regarding that. I believe you said that you spoke with attorney-at-law Vasic some two years ago. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How long did the conversation take, since you said you didn't take any notes. Do you remember whether he kept any notes on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: He must have been keeping notes. The first conversation was in Nusiceva Street. So it must have been over two years ago. And he asked me some questions, he asked me, "Do you remember this and that?" And I said, well, maybe some other people can respond better to that. Perhaps a month later, we gathered the people I assembled at the command of the then Guards Brigade at Dedinje in Bulevar Mira Street 92. And we went through those issues with Vasic. Then we dispersed. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How about last summer or last year, when you spoke to Mr. Vasic? What was the main topic of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: The main topic of that conversation, and of the conversations previously, although it wasn't mentioned here today, was the way the briefings went between the 18th and the 24th, what happened on the 18th, the 19th, the 20th, how, and then as two years ago I told him the same thing. I hope I don't need to repeat. And he showed me a paper, a piece of paper, and I can say this, and this piece of paper pertained to Radoje Trifunovic, and to be honest, I was sick to see what he wrote down. I told him this has got nothing to do with anything, that this is untrue, and then in addition to the family problems I had at the time, I just wanted to leave, yet I stayed, although my spouse was sick at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, one of the topics was whether you will testify or not in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. We discussed this in detail as well, especially during the last three or four months. My spouse was operated on the 25th of May, and I told you on the phone that I couldn't come at that time. First of all, there was someone sick in my family and also the fact that I was disarmed. I was stripped of my papers. Because I was taught to win by using arguments, and this is what I taught others. This is how I lived my life. I was taught that only through honest work anything good can be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic. As you stated yesterday in the afternoon and today, you spoke with me as well.

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You answered to some of my questions today. Was that a topic of our discussion or did we discuss something else?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't discuss anything apart from the questions you put today, and I provided you with answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And to conclude, since you were told that you came here to testify falsely, to aid Mrksic and some others, I wanted to ask you this: Did you tell the truth here and the things you said today, does it all come from your memory? Is this what you remember?

utterances.speaker: BORISA GLUSCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I only spoke the truth and nothing but the truth. And only when I was 100 per cent sure that it was so indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gluscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Gluscevic, you'll be pleased to know that completes the questions that will be asked of you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give, and you are now free to return to your home and your family and affairs. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, perhaps we will deal with some formalities. Mr. Domazet, I take it in view of what has transpired that that concludes the evidence that you have available?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We conclude our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And of course, that's subject to the leave that we did give you, should you wish to pursue it, of seeking leave to call one witness later on who may at the moment be subject to a health problem. Very well. The case of Mr. Mrksic is now closed. Now, Mr. Domazet, the health position of your client would suggest that unless he consents to the trial proceeding in his absence, that we would need to adjourn for some days this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am afraid this will be the case. As I stated at the beginning, I didn't speak to Mr. Mrksic personally but he spoke with Mr. Vasic, and he told him that he wished to be present during the Radic Defence case evidence. However, he gave his consent to go through with this witness for today, and he agreed to the opening statement to be heard today. I don't know whether he changed his mind in the meantime, but this is what I was told by Mr. Vasic, who unfortunately is not with us here in the courtroom today because he felt tired, but this is what I was supposed to convey to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Borovic, I'm afraid, in the circumstances, looking forward to your witnesses for the moment, that it would appear that we have to delay a few days, because of Mr. Mrksic's health, the commencement of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expected such a reaction on the part of the first accused, precisely at the moment when I was to start presenting our evidence. Therefore, I believe you should put an end to such slowing down of these proceedings with all due respect for Mr. Domazet, and there is for the following reason. We lost 20 days in August. We kept talking about the postponement of the proceedings, and witnesses were called at the last moment. Once I put my schedule together, once my first witness was here and I was about to start proofing him today, of course, I'm sorry for Mr. Mrksic's health condition, but today, when I visited Mr. Radic, I saw him taking his walk in the courtyard of the prison, he wasn't resting; therefore, I have a suggestion to make. Despite the recommendation issued that he should be absent for another week, we'll have to decide yet again what will happen next. This is another unknown in front of us. I do believe that Mr. Mrksic could be able to follow the proceedings provide there had is a videolink and a telephone line to his attorneys during the breaks, and this was used in the Samac case. This would not cause any postponement or delay in these proceedings because some of the accused do not waste any more time in The Hague. I apologise for this expression but this was my personal view. Hence, my suggestion is, provided the Chamber can decide in favour of this, that we continue so that I don't have to send my witnesses away again, because I already have additional problems of seeing those witnesses off, then I have to ask for another permission by the military authorities to approve their leave for some of the witnesses are not pensioners but professional soldiers. All in all, I remember the last Thursday and today we only had one witness. So we've lost our momentum for the past two weeks and now we have to wait for the next Monday and God knows how many more days. I apologise for maybe being harsh in trying to protect the rights of my client but this is his view as well. We would like to start, and we chose to have as few witnesses as possible, although we could have put forth 35, but due to the fairness of the case and given all the principles here, I believe our requests are not unfounded. Hence, I believe I can start with my opening statement today but this will of course depend on your guidance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps just to inform the Chamber, I can reiterate what I said last week, and I discussed this with my client today as well, I told you about another intervention that he should have, just so that we shouldn't have to go into private session again, I won't go into details as to how long it should take, et cetera. But in any case, he agreed that no other postponements should be introduced in these proceedings. Perhaps on the day it should happen, and I don't want to mention the date due to security reasons, perhaps on that day he could be present in the morning but I didn't receive any assurances of that. As regards the other two days I mentioned, he would be absent from the sessions on those two days. In case there are sessions on those two days, which is still to be approved, this would make our work more difficult, given the relative significance of Mr. Radic's evidence and the evidence of some other witnesses, and we would have to go through the transcript rather than being here in the courtroom. Of course, this is a problem to us as well to have our client absent, but we also have other accused and we don't want to interfere with the speediness of these proceedings. We want the deadlines met, and we hope that this would not be taken against the number of days given to us to present our case. I know that all of us in this courtroom think along the same lines, that we should conclude this year. Therefore, I don't think the Chamber would want to see anything happen to the detriment of our defence, especially in terms of the number of days that we were given for our case. This is why Mr. Sljivancanin wishes to see this proceedings move on. Should you need any other medical information, I'm prepared to be of assistance, although what I know and what my client knows still is very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Counsel will be aware that the progress of the trial since the close of the Prosecution case has been interrupted for two reasons, reasons that are of concern to everybody because of the resulting delays in the completion of the trial. The first reason was a significant heart attack that was suffered by the lead counsel for Mr. Mrksic. Fortunately, Mr. Vasic has been able to rejoin the Mrksic Defence in recent weeks. The second is a health condition which affected Mr. Mrksic himself and which led to surgery of some significance last week. Mr. Mrksic is in the process of recovering from that surgery. The present medical opinion we have is that he would need seven days to recover, subject to further review at the end of that time. Counsel will also be aware that under the rules, a trial cannot proceed in the absence of an accused unless the accused consents to that occurring. For reasons that have been explained by Mr. Domazet, Mr. Mrksic does not consent to the evidence to be led from Mr. Radic being heard in his absence. As has been indicated by Mr. Lukic, there is also imminent a need for some surgery to his client, or some intervention, surgery overstates the position, and that is likely to occur in the near future. Mr. Sljivancanin is prepared for some of the trial to proceed in his absence but he too desires to be present during the evidence of Mr. Radic and the evidence as we hear it of at least two other of Mr. Radic's witnesses. The only way of getting out of this difficulty is that which has been suggested by Mr. Borovic, which is to arrange a videolink between the courtroom and where Mr. Mrksic is resting, with a telephone connection to his counsel so that he is able to watch the proceedings, hear the evidence, and communicate with his counsel. The Chamber already has under way inquiries as to whether it is feasible for that connection to be made in the next day or so, and we must also, of course, confirm that that would be consistent with his medical condition. We may be able to get answers to those questions in the course of tomorrow. If it is possible to proceed in that way, we would do so. It may even be possible to do that on Wednesday. It's too early yet to be sure. That, though, will not overcome the problem of Mr. Sljivancanin at the time that, whenever it is, that his medical procedure needs to occur. So that it may be necessary for that reason to interrupt even the proceedings being continued with Mr. Mrksic watching by videolink. That is something we needn't resolve today despite the very cooperative hand signal of Mr. Sljivancanin a moment ago, because it's not yet clear whether it will be feasible to have a videolink and for that to be consistent with Mr. Mrksic's recovery. If it is, we will then look at the detailed problem of Mr. Sljivancanin's relatively short need for absence. We will therefore, of course, hear you this evening, Mr. Borovic, if that is still convenient, in opening your case. You will have to confirm whether there is time enough for you to do that, but if there is, we certainly appreciate your ready cooperation in that regard. We will not at the moment see any point in trying to sit tomorrow, because it is clear that without Mr. Mrksic's consent, we cannot achieve any arrangements in time for tomorrow. It may be possible, if everything comes together, to sit again on Wednesday. You will have to be told as time progresses whether that is feasible or not. If the worst comes to the worst, it would appear that we would not be able to sit until next Monday morning -- Monday afternoon. Should that happen, and that's, it seems, the worst that could happen at the moment, I could indicate, Mr. Borovic, that we already have in place arrangements for us to sit longer hours on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of next week. We have been able to make those arrangements today because a courtroom has become free. So if necessary, we can sit longer hours next week to try and help you with the problems that you are now facing with witnesses being needed at a later time than you had anticipated. And we'll do all that we can to help you with those difficulties, if that is the way things work out. So I regret this but for the moment it would appear we must anticipate that we will not be able to sit tomorrow, and that it may prove possible to sit on Wednesday and days following, subject should the two overlap with the need to take into account Mr. Sljivancanin's procedure. And if the time is lost, and we can help in making it up, we'll do what we can next week and we've been able to make arrangements for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and we'll continue to look for other opportunities to be able to sit longer hours to help you catch up during the period of your case. We must now adjourn for the break. That would leave an hour, Mr. Borovic. Is that sufficient for your opening? It is? Thank you for that. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, we come now to the opening of your client's case. His rights and entitlements I know have been fully explained to him by you and we leave it to you then to proceed to present the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, and learned friends, the Defence is aware of and shall abide by the guidance issued by the Honourable Trial Chamber that the opening statement should be brief and that we should only deal with relevant matters. Through the opening statement, we are not going to assess evidence and have it confronted. That is to say that through this opening statement, the Defence shall, in the briefest possible terms, make it possible for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to follow what will be presented as evidence in the Defence case of Miroslav Radic. As I have already stated to all the participants in these proceedings, Miroslav Radic is going to call a total of eight witnesses, including himself. Out of that, two witnesses are 92 bis witnesses and we have one witness who is a military expert. Therefore, an expert witness. Now, why did the Defence of Miroslav Radic decide on such a seemingly small number of witnesses? Just as I said, precise -- primarily because they are going to be witnesses that are relevant to his position in these criminal proceedings. I am not calling witnesses with regard to general matters because we have heard enough of that. The Defence thinks that through the Prosecution witnesses, it introduced a great deal of evidence that actually works in favour of the Defence, and that that will indeed do. There is yet another reason, as we expect witnesses of the third accused person, who will deal with many matters that were referred to during expert testimony, they are probably going to testify as they did through their statements to the Prosecution. That may be a favourable circumstance, and I believe that in this way, I have saved quite a bit of time in these proceedings. Miroslav Radic decided to be a witness in his own case, and I'm aware of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and I know that it is not something that is akin to what was the case elsewhere, that he is trying to give evidence in terms of his innocence only. In addition to that, which is not the only thing that I'm referring to, he is not going to avail himself of the privilege to hear all other witnesses first and then benefit from their testimony and then testify on behalf of his own defence before this Trial Chamber. I think that the Trial Chamber should give special weight to this when assessing the evidence. That is the assessment of Defence counsel, and we will see what the view of the Trial Chamber will be with regard to this matter. Miroslav Radic, together with Mrksic and Veselin Sljivancanin, stands accused before this Tribunal for grave violations in accordance with the Statute. He is charged with persecutions, extermination, murder, torture, inhumane acts, all this as crimes against humanity, and he is charged for murder, torture, cruel treatment, which are all violations of the laws and customs of war, grave violations of the laws and customs of war. In terms of individual responsibility, the indictment charges him with participation in joint criminal enterprise with the other accused in this courtroom, and with persons by the name of Stanko Vujanovic, Miroljub Vujovic, and other known and unknown persons, as stated in paragraph 7 of the indictment, members of the Serb forces. Also, the accused is charged with responsibility in accordance with Article 7(3) of the Statute, that as a superior he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit acts or had already done so, and that he as the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. Over the next few days, Miroslav Radic shall, through the witnesses that the Defence has called before this Trial Chamber, will present their knowledge regarding the events that pertain to specific charges in the indictment, and they will explain the role that Miroslav Radic had in these events to the extent to which he took part in this or they will confirm that he did not participate in this, to be more precise. The Defence will prove through witnesses and primarily through the witness Miroslav Radic that he was not a member of any joint criminal enterprise, something that he was not aware of at all. He was not aware of its existence at all. And therefore, Miroslav Radic, together with other persons, known as unknown, could not have shared a common objective, which is very important from a legal point of view, of the said enterprise, as mentioned in paragraph 5 of this indictment. Let me just repeat: The indictment says that the objective of this joint criminal enterprise was the persecution of Croats and other non-Serbs who, after the fall of Vukovar, were present in the Vukovar Hospital. That is the position taken by the Prosecution. Persecution was committed by way of murder, torture, cruel treatment, exterminations and others inhuman acts, which is punishable according to Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute. Miroslav Radic was not a member of any joint criminal enterprise, and he was not aware of the existence of any such thing, and therefore he could not have had the requisite mens rea in accordance with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal with regard to any one of the crimes that he is being charged with. In general terms, the Defence repels every possibility as mentioned in paragraph 8 of the indictment, the crimes that Miroslav Radic has been charged with were the natural and foreseeable consequence of carrying out a joint criminal enterprise and that, I repeat, the accused was aware that the crimes were a possible effect of its commission. During the Defence case of Miroslav Radic, we will show that in contrast to what paragraph 8 of the indictment says, he did not work in concert with or through any individual that is mentioned as a member of a joint criminal enterprise either through that person or through other persons. So with regard to all of this, it is precisely Miroslav Radic who will best be in a position to present his position. In accordance with all of this, the Defence cannot agree that Miroslav Radic was either independently or in concert with other known and unknown participants in a joint criminal enterprise, a participant in its commission or, rather, implementation as described in paragraph 10 of the indictment, specifically under (a), that he directed, commanded, controlled or otherwise exercised effective control over Serb forces as referred to in paragraph 7 of the indictment, which in the view of the Prosecution are responsible for what happened to persons whose names are mentioned in the annex to the indictment. Of course, we are going to hear Miroslav Radic as a witness with regard to this. We are also going to hear an officer who was his superior officer and whose name is on the 65 ter list, and we are going to call a very credible witness, a military expert, with regard to all of these matters. We will be in a position to hear him, and through him we are going to tender a great deal of written evidence, documents primarily of a military nature, and you will see what the position of the Defence is with regard to subparagraph (a). Then in paragraph 10 it also says that he personally participated in the removal and selection of about 400 persons from the Vukovar Hospital knowing or having reason to know that these persons would be subjected to further persecution and murder. Your Honours, the indictment even mentions the figure of 300. There are different figures, but that is totally irrelevant now, because we are going to have a clear and unequivocal statement made by Miroslav Radic himself, and I hope that this fair agreement that exists between me and the third accused person will lead to witnesses that I will be able to question in detail. And I've already said several times, if the Prosecution gave up on some of their witnesses, then the Defence of the first accused person gave up on certain witnesses, whereas I waited for the proper moment, namely for some other Defence to do that, all of it with a view to shortening the time of these proceedings. Then, after having become aware that the criminal acts charged in this indictment had been completed, he took steps to hide and conceal these crimes. That is what is alleged in the indictment, but that will be dealt with in a separate part of this opening statement. It will be quite clear, and I think that so far it has become quite clear, even to the Prosecution, that paragraph 16 of the indictment is untrue and that Stanko Vujanovic, commander of one of the companies of the TO, the Territorial Defence, was not under the command of Miroslav Radic in any way. In contrast to that allegation and paragraph 40 of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, we see that even the Prosecution's expert witness shows that the situation is actually the other way around. But we are going to call witnesses who are going to refute that. That is to say, all the witnesses who can speak about this shall do so, as well as the military expert that we intend to call. Miroslav Radic was not advised directly or indirectly, and nor could he have been aware, that members of certain Serb forces were threatening to harm or that they had already caused harm to Croats and other non-Serbs who after the fall of Vukovar, for various reasons, and motives, were in the Vukovar Hospital. Therefore, Miroslav Radic did not know and there was no reason for him to know that someone, for whom we still have to prove was his subordinate, and that person was not, that that person was preparing to commit the crimes alleged in the indictment. Or worse yet, that those crimes had already been committed, without Miroslav Radic undertaking the necessary measures to prevent them or to punish the perpetrators. It will become clear through our Defence case concerning the circumstance and the information that exists that the Prosecution has no evidence, no proof. By presenting our evidence we will contest the allegations of paragraph 26, that Miroslav Radic, together with the other participants of the JCE, held the so-called regular meetings in the house in Nova Street number 81. Such allegation is untrue, and the house, owned by Stanko Vujanovic's house -- father, could not have been an operational centre, a place where military operations were planned pertaining to Vukovar. Not even the OTP witnesses were able to corroborate that. Quite the contrary. It would be very difficult to plan such operations in or at an observation post of a company commander. If we stick to the military rules, and if they are used as the basis for some allegations made by the OTP in the individual stages of the proceedings, then we have to stick to them completely, including the rules of service of platoons and companies. Through our military expert, we will also expand on that topic. We will explain clearly what an observation post is. We heard one military professional who was not an expert but was one of the OTP witnesses, who, to a large extent, explained what we will attempt to present to this Chamber using the documents that we will seek to tender through this witness. The company commander we are talking about is tasked with implementing the orders of his superiors. A company commander is a commander at the -- of the lowest rank. According to the JNA hierarchy, Miroslav Radic was not a komandant as we could often hear in this proceedings. But rather he was a komandir. This is a substantive difference in the rules of service, and in real terms. As stated by the military expert that we will see here, the commander of the 3rd Motorised Company of the 1st Motorised Brigade, Captain Miroslav Radic, according to the documents of the command of the 1st Motorised Brigade of JOD 1, during the combat activities performed a functional duty as well, this being the coordinator of the 3rd Assault Group. In the initial stages, he cooperated with the -- some Vukovar TO units, this being the detachments of Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica. The orders issued by commander of the 1st Motorised Brigade were simultaneously received by Captain Radic as well as by the TO commander, Dusan Jaksic, and this was later Miroljub Vujovic, as well as the commander of the Leva Supoderica detachment, Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, as of the moment when these TO detachments were attached, and this is a military term, to the 1st Motorised Battalion, JOD 1. Therefore, Captain Miroslav Radic was not superior to the commanders of the aforementioned TO detachments and this is what we will prove, not only by evidence but also by the opinion of our military expert. The paragraph of the indictment in which the Prosecutor asserts that Miroslav Radic, inter alia, was present when allegedly Vojislav Seselj in the house owned by Stanko Vujanovic's father stated quote/unquote, not a single Ustasha is to leave Vukovar alive. In the pre-trial brief, paragraph 44, the Prosecutor asserts that on that occasion, the goal or the intention to kill the non-Serb opponents began taking on a new form among the members of the JCE. We heard some OTP witnesses drawing on various sources stating that this may have been said in one house or in the street, but there were great discrepancies as to their statements whether Radic was present. We have to state a clear position as regards that, and we will hear Miroslav Radic's to begin our case with. The indictment charges Miroslav Radic with selection of detainees who were put on the buses in front of the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November, 1991, as well as Miroslav Radic taking 15 people off the bus and returning them to the hospital, most likely because they were members of the hospital staff. These are two important items. In our view, this is just an improvisation, for want of a better word, from paragraph 34 of the indictment, because as early as in the pre-trial brief, in paragraph 119, it is not clearly stated what Miroslav Radic precisely did on that occasion, if he was there at all. And it is our position that at the moment of selection, he wasn't there. He did not participate. I believe this may be one of the reasons for withdrawing some of the witnesses from the list of the OTP, because they didn't have other witnesses who could have claimed they were part of this selection process, and there was no one else who could have said, "I returned those 15 people to the Vukovar Hospital." Irrespective of that, with all due respect for the Chamber and our learned friends from the Prosecution, we will attempt to persuade you of the -- of these items as being completely unfounded. To conclude, the indictment charges Miroslav Radic that the next day, on the 21st of November, together with Stanko Vujanovic, in his father's house, discussed the events of the previous night and that he took no measures to punish his subordinates but rather that he even tried to cover up the crime. This Defence will show that such Prosecution allegations are incorrect and that due to the development of events during and after the fall of Vukovar, Miroslav Radic did not have any knowledge as to the events that took place between the 20th and the 21st of November, 1991. Having that in mind, he couldn't have been able to undertake the necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators. We have already advised our learned friends through our briefs of the witnesses we intend to call and the evidence we intend to lead. And hopefully, these people will, beyond any doubt, confirm our position. The issue of the existence of the armed conflict can be in dispute because the Prosecutor claims that throughout the former Yugoslavia, at the material time, there was a state of armed conflict. One needs to be cautious when discussing this and to see whether this armed conflict included the whole territory of the former Yugoslavia or only a part of it, and whether we indeed are talking about an armed conflict or a rebellion in one part of that sovereign state. This conflict or rebellion was incited and staged by illegal units which were illegally armed by illegally importing weapons. We will not dwell too much on this issue, but we hope that through the expert's opinion and the evidence we will lead, we hope to clarify that issue. The Defence contests the allegation that Miroslav Radic, as a member of the JCE, by acting or failing to act, contributed to the realisation of the JCE plans. When it comes to crimes against humanity our client is charged with, it is stipulated that such acting or failing to act formed part of a widespread and systematic attack on Croatian and other non-Serb populations in a large part of Croatia, including Vukovar. As we will hear from the accused's evidence as well as the evidence of our military expert, we will be able to establish that the joint preconditions for the existence of crimes against humanity have not been met. Such preconditions need to be met cumulatively, and especially the subjective precondition, this being that the accused was aware that there was an attack on civilian population and that crimes were part of that attack. The accused himself will explain what his view of the situation and his understanding was, as well as the other witnesses on our list. This Defence will focus on trying to show before this Tribunal that Miroslav Radic commanded only over the soldiers of his company, or rather that he commanded the assault group. We will also seek to explain that the local TO as well as the other units mentioned were an independent body. We seek to corroborate this through some of the OTP witnesses' testimony as well, and we will also have some of the witnesses called here by the first accused, and we will try to explain as well that during the operations in Vukovar these units cooperated with the JNA but that Miroslav Radic had no effective control over those units, especially not after the cessation of hostilities on the 18th of November in 1991. After you've heard our evidence, it will be clear that Miroslav Radic had no effective control over -- as stipulated in paragraph 247 of the pre-trial brief of the OTP, over some of the perpetrators of the crimes at Ovcara. The engagement of the 3rd Motorised Company as the 3rd Assault Group in combat activities in the operation at Vukovar lasted until the takeover of Milovo Brdo on the 10th of November, 1991, according to the log of the 1st Motorised Brigade command, and until the 14th November 1991, at the latest; that is, until the decision of the OG South commander, strictly confidential number 398-1, at 8.00 on the 14th of November, 1991. As of that moment, all TO units have been withdrawn from the 3rd Assault Group and they haven't been under the command of Captain Miroslav Radic. Witnesses will confirm that Miroslav Radic abided by the principles of singleness of command and unity of command as well as his obligation to implement decisions and orders, as being one of the basic principles of the doctrine of the then armed forces of the SFRY. The witnesses you will hear, Your Honours, will also address the allegations of paragraph 22. They will show that he completely implemented the orders of his superior and that he acted completely in accordance with the then rules of service. He also acted according to high professional and personal standards and principles due to which he enjoyed a very favourable reputation among the JNA soldiers he commanded. Not a single OTP witness, no matter how uncomfortable they were, still could not have said anything contrary to such traits of Miroslav Radic. We'll hear several witnesses on this issue, among which of course the military expert, who, in his report, will attempt to show that Miroslav Radic has proven himself to be a successful commander in the Vukovar operation as recorded in the official documents of the 1st Motorised Brigade, JOD 1, and he received a high commendation once he returned to Belgrade. He received a commendation for bravery and an extraordinary promotion into the rank of captain first-class. This commendation was in keeping with the laws and regulations on the promotion and commendations of military personnel. This is a very important issue. And this was addressed also by the OTP military expert. When analysing various statements and evidence as regards that, and when we put all that before the military expert, he had nothing to say. He only principally disputed some of the allegations of the Defence, but we will have yet another opportunity when the Chamber puts the two reports together and compares them. This will also include some witness testimony as regards the military doctrine. The indictment as well as the pre-trial brief of the Prosecutor is, to a large extent, based on witness statements of those witnesses that were originally put on the OTP witness list. However, we were not given the opportunity to hear some of those witnesses. The reasons for that are unknown -- are known only to them but I also believe these reasons will be known to the Trial Chamber as well, once we indeed see those witnesses and once we hear what those people have to say concerning some additional issues that needed to have been discussed. As promised, I won't take too much of your time. My opening statement is rather general. Among the material forwarded to the Prosecutor, we specified as regards what circumstances each witness will testify, including Miroslav Radic himself, and we also attempted to show to them what will be dealt with by our military expert. On the basis of all that, the place and role of Miroslav Radic will be clearer, because as the commander of the 1st Company, I believe should not have been made part of this indictment. To conclude, I wanted to quote my learned friend, Mr. Moore, on page 12448. This was during Witness Danilovic's testimony, and I believe he was quite right to have reacted emotionally. He told him that the Chief of Staff is the eyes and ears of his commander. He has to be able to take control of the situation should something happen. So this is not just an ordinary company commander. An OTP position towards a company commander, and this being Mr. Miroslav Radic, is illustrative enough concerning the events at Ovcara. What we have to do as Defence, and I believe we will manage to prove that, and I will also be glad to be right to prove the Prosecutor wrong, was -- will be to address the allegations from the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, before we adjourn for the evening, Mr. Lukic, there was a matter you wished to raise, the statement -- the admissibility of the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that Mr. Moore had asked me to wait for Weiner to be present in the courtroom -- Mr. Weiner, because he deals with that particular subject, but I can present my own argumentation now, if you wish to hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we thought it was something that parties needed to get out of the way. Can that be done tonight, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Weiner is dealing with the topic. I believe that he and Mr. Lukic were talking about the matter. It may well be it can be resolved outside court. I know not, but I would be loathe to argue it without the points that Mr. Weiner wishes to deal with. We did not know, of course, that this week might be aborted. One hopes that it will not be aborted. The one thing that can be said, however, it is not a topic that is burning with urgency. Of course, all topics are, I understand that, but it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The end of this case is burning with urgency, Mr. Moore, but I think in view of what you said, it must wait until a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will not be able to sit tomorrow, just to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We did, on Wednesday or early Thursday last week, indicate that the decision would be delivered on Friday on the question of the use of statements in cross-examination by the Prosecution. Following that, further written submissions were received. They are being considered and will be taken into account and that has delayed that decision a short time. But it should be in place, Mr. Borovic, before your client gives evidence. In those circumstances, I think the time has come to adjourn this evening. There seems no prospect of us being able to sit tomorrow, and we will advise parties if it becomes possible to sit on Wednesday or any day following during the week, on the basis discussed earlier today. Thank you very much. We now adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Radic and Sljivancanin entered court]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.41 p.m.
